_: Stage 11 · Nuance — N2 opens. Steps 44–46. Spliced by build-stage3.py. Blueprint in stage-11-blueprint-v1.md, approved by Lloyd Session 18.
_theme: Stage 9 taught the learner to argue; Stage 10 to say it precisely. Stage 11 is where the language starts holding its shape under pressure — refusing politely, speaking at ceremonies, writing for the record. The register climbs and the stakes are other people's opinion of you.
_status: AI-AUTHORED, NOT REVIEWED. Reviewer batch P. The formal register is where a small wrongness costs most — にあたって vs に際して nuance and かねます in customer speech want the closest native read.

new_steps.note: Stage 11 opens. N3 could refuse (わけにはいかない) and regret (ばよかった). These are the adult forms: obligation you accept with distaste, refusal wrapped for customers, and possibilities you rule out entirely.

points.en: no choice but to — and I mind

exp.what: しかない said there was no other option and stayed casual about it. ざるを得ない says the same thing in a stiffer collar, and adds a feeling: I am doing this because refusing is not available, and you can hear that I would have refused. ざる is the old negative — 'not-doing' — so the bones read 'cannot get away with not doing.'
exp.build: Verb ない-stem + ざるを得ない: 行かざるを得ない, 認めざるを得ない. する becomes せざるを得ない — the same old-Japanese stem that gave you せず. It conjugates like an い-less verb: past 〜ざるを得なかった.
exp.when: Written and formal spoken Japanese: reports, apologies, meetings. Accepting overtime, conceding a point, cancelling something you promised. It signals reluctance without complaining — which is exactly the register Japanese workplaces run on.
exp.watch: It needs real pressure behind it. 食べざるを得ない about a snack is comedy. And keep the する exception straight: しざるを得ない is wrong, せざるを得ない is the form — the ず/ざる family always reaches back to せ.

ex: 予算がないので、計画を諦めざるを得ない。
With no budget, we have no choice but to give up the plan.
部長の命令だから、引き受けざるを得なかった。
It was the director's order, so I had no choice but to take it on.

exp.what: Not 'it's hard' and not 'I can't' — the route itself is missing. 直しようがない: there is no way the fixing could even be attempted. The pattern removes the method, not the will.
exp.build: Verb ます-stem + ようがない: 言いようがない, 連絡しようがない. The よう here is the same one as in 言いよう — 'way of saying' — with がない bolted on: the way doesn't exist.
exp.when: When the missing piece is a means: no address, no parts, no words. 説明しようがない is the honest answer when the facts themselves are missing, and it is gentler than 説明できない because it blames the situation, not your ability.
exp.watch: Contrast with できない: 泳げない means you never learned; 泳ぎようがない means the pool is empty. If a listener could reply 'but you could if…', ようがない was the wrong claim.

ex: 住所が分からないので、知らせようがない。
I don't know the address, so there's no way to inform them.
ここまで壊れていると、直しようがない。
Broken this badly, there's no way to fix it.

points.en: cannot quite — and its dangerous twin

exp.what: かねる is refusal in a suit: 分かりかねます means 'I am not in a position to know that,' said across a counter with a bow in it. かねない is its mirror and it flips the meaning entirely — 'might well (do something bad)': 事故になりかねない, this could easily end in an accident.
exp.build: Verb ます-stem + かねる for the polite cannot: 致しかねます, お答えしかねます. Same stem + かねない for the might-well: なりかねない, 忘れかねない. The negative-looking one is the affirmative threat — that is the trap.
exp.when: かねる is service Japanese: you will hear it every time a clerk refuses you something. かねない belongs in warnings — always about outcomes nobody wants.
exp.watch: The pair inverts English instincts: かねる (looks positive) = can't; かねない (looks negative) = might. And かねない never takes good outcomes: 合格しかねない is wrong — the pattern smells of trouble by definition.

ex: その質問にはお答えし かねます。
I'm afraid I cannot answer that question.
このままでは、大きな問題になりかねない。
At this rate, it could well turn into a serious problem.

exp.what: One old ending, two jobs. On your own actions it is a vow of not-doing: 二度と行くまい, I'll never go again. About the world it is a formal 'probably not': 雨は降るまい, it will hardly rain. Both readings share a stiffness — まい belongs to writing and to speeches, not to texting.
exp.build: Dictionary form + まい for godan verbs: 行くまい, 言うまい. Ichidan and the irregulars prefer the stem: 食べまい, するまい／しまい, 来るまい／来（こ）まい — variation exists and the dictionary-form version is always safe.
exp.when: Resolutions after a bad experience (二度と〜まい is the set shape), and written prediction where だろう would sound too soft. You will read it far more than you will say it.
exp.watch: まい is negative already — 行かないまい doubles the negative and breaks. And the vow reading only works on YOUR actions; 彼は行くまい can only be the 'probably not' sense.

ex: あんな店には二度と行くまい。
I will never go to that place again.
彼はもう戻るまいと、みんなが思っていた。
Everyone thought he would surely not come back.

exp.what: A subtraction marker for situations: 冗談抜きで, joking aside; 社長抜きで, without the president present. What follows proceeds with the named thing deliberately removed.
exp.build: Noun + 抜きで, or Noun + を抜きにして for the heavier version: お世辞を抜きにして言うと… The verb 抜く — pull out — is doing the work: the noun has been pulled out of the situation.
exp.when: Setting ground rules for a conversation (formality aside, budget aside), and ordering food without something — わさび抜きで is the everyday face of the same grammar.
exp.watch: It removes something expected. 抜きで on a thing nobody assumed was there reads as strange — the pattern implies the default included it.

ex: 冗談抜きで、締め切りは明日です。
Joking aside, the deadline is tomorrow.
今日は仕事の話を抜きにして、楽しみましょう。
Let's leave work talk out of it today and enjoy ourselves.

exp.what: Three fossils of the classical negative survive in modern formal Japanese, and Stage 11 uses all of them: ず (Step 40's 〜ずに), ざる (ざるを得ない), and まい. They are one system, not three exceptions.
exp.build: All three build on the ない-stem: 行かず・行かざる・(行くまい stands apart, taking the dictionary form). する reaches back to せ for the first two — せず, せざる — which is why しざる sounds wrong to every native ear.
exp.when: Recognising them turns formal writing from a wall into a pattern: 〜ざる者 in proverbs, 〜ず in headlines, まい in editorials. Producing them, you only need the three fixed shapes this stage teaches.
exp.watch: The trap is regularising する: しずに and しざるを得ない are the learner errors the checker will flag. Old grammar keeps old stems.

ex: 働かざる者、食うべからず。
He who does not work shall not eat. (the proverb — ざる in the wild)
何も言わず、部屋を出た。
Without a word, I left the room.

exp.what: Write a four-line refusal: the situation, the impossibility (ようがない or ざるを得ない), the polite cannot (かねます), and one alternative you CAN offer.
exp.build: Line shape to steal: 残念ですが、今回は引き受けざるを得ない事情があり、お受けし かねます。代わりに〜はいかがでしょうか。
exp.when: This is the single most reusable email shape in working Japanese — declining without closing the door.
exp.watch: Keep the feeling out of the middle lines. The reluctance lives inside ざるを得ない already; adding とても悲しいです on top makes it about you.

ex: 申し訳ありませんが、その日は出席し かねます。
I'm terribly sorry, but I'm unable to attend that day.

new_steps.note: N5 pinned actions to clock time; Step 19 walked time's edges. This step is about OCCASIONS — the marked moments a life is measured in — and the formal timing grammar that ceremonies, contracts and announcements run on.

exp.what: とき says when something happens; に際して says the moment is an OCCASION — marked, formal, worth a sentence of its own. 契約に際して is not 'when contracting' but 'on the occasion of entering this contract.'
exp.build: Noun or dictionary-form verb + に際して: ご利用に際して, 出発に際して. Written notices prefer に際しての before a noun: 入学に際しての注意.
exp.when: Contracts, ceremonies, first days, official notices — anywhere the moment itself has weight. It is the phrase on the first page of every terms-of-service you will never read.
exp.watch: Everyday moments reject it: 昼ご飯に際して is a joke. If とき would do, use とき — に際して spends formality, and spending it on lunch reads as sarcasm.

ex: ご契約に際して、以下の書類が必要です。
On entering the contract, the following documents are required.
出発に際して、一言ご挨拶申し上げます。
On the occasion of departure, allow me a word of greeting.

exp.what: The sibling of に際して, standing a half-step earlier: にあたって faces a significant undertaking about to begin, and usually introduces preparation or resolve. 新学期を迎えるにあたって — as the new term is about to open.
exp.build: Noun or dictionary-form verb + にあたって（は）: 開店にあたって, 面接を受けるにあたって. Speeches love it as an opener.
exp.when: Kick-off speeches, prefaces, the first slide of a presentation. It frames what follows as the preparation the moment deserves.
exp.watch: Both this and に際して need positive-or-neutral undertakings — 事故にあたって is broken, because an accident is not a threshold anyone stands at deliberately. For bad events, plain とき carries no such expectation.

ex: 面接を受けるにあたって、会社のことをよく調べた。
Ahead of the interview, I researched the company thoroughly.
新生活を始めるにあたって、荷物を減らした。
On starting the new life, I cut down my belongings.

exp.what: てから says 'after'; て以来 says 'ever since — and it has stayed that way.' 引っ越して以来 opens a state that began at the move and still holds at the moment of speaking.
exp.build: て-form + 以来: 卒業して以来, 会って以来. Also Noun + 以来: 入社以来, あれ以来. The following clause must describe something continuing, not a one-time event.
exp.when: Catching up (あれ以来どう？), résumés and self-introductions (入社以来ずっと営業です), and any sentence whose point is an unbroken stretch.
exp.watch: One-time results break it: 引っ越して以来、机を買った is wrong — buying happened once. If the second half could take ずっと, て以来 fits; if not, てから was the word.

ex: 日本に来て以来、ずっとこの町に住んでいます。
Ever since coming to Japan, I've lived in this town.
卒業して以来、彼とは会っていない。
I haven't seen him since graduation.

exp.what: Two events packed so close the first hadn't clearly ended: ベルが鳴るか鳴らないかのうちに, before the bell had even finished ringing. The grammar performs the overlap by asking 'did it happen or not yet?' and answering 'both.'
exp.build: Same verb, affirmative + ないかのうちに: 言うか言わないかのうちに, 着くか着かないかのうちに. The second event follows immediately.
exp.when: Storytelling, mostly — it is the pattern for eagerness and abruptness. The train doors, the starting gun, the child out of the door before goodbye landed.
exp.watch: The two verbs must be the SAME verb — 鳴るか終わらないかのうちに breaks the mechanism. And the second event must be actual and instant; a slow consequence wants と or たとたん instead.

ex: 乾杯が終わるか終わらないかのうちに、料理が運ばれてきた。
The food arrived before the toast had even finished.
ドアが開くか開かないかのうちに、猫が飛び出した。
The cat shot out before the door was barely open.

exp.what: A hard sequencing gate: until X is done, Y cannot happen. 契約してからでないと、鍵は渡せません — no key until the contract is signed. The pattern states a precondition and closes the door on shortcuts.
exp.build: て-form + からでないと + a negative or impossible outcome: 確認してからでないと分かりません. The heavier written variant is てからでなければ.
exp.when: Rules, procedures, counters — everywhere Japan's love of correct order becomes grammar. It is the polite mechanics behind '手続きが先です.'
exp.watch: The second half must be negative or blocked (できない, 分からない, 渡せません). A positive follow-up wants plain てから: 食べてから行く, no gate needed.

ex: 上司に相談してからでないと、お返事できません。
I can't reply until I've consulted my boss.
書類が届いてからでないと、更新の手続きは始められない。
The renewal process can't start until the documents arrive.

exp.what: Japan marks thresholds with 式 — a ceremony with assigned seats and a script. 入学式 and 卒業式 bracket every school year; 入社式 opens working life each April 1st, whole cohorts in identical suits; 結婚式 needs no translation. The suffix 式 on a noun is a reliable signal that attendance, dress and timing are all decided for you.
exp.build: The vocabulary cluster: 司会 runs the room, 乾杯 is the one moment everyone speaks at once, 挨拶 is the speech genre the timing grammar of this step was built for — に際して and にあたって live in ceremony speeches.
exp.when: You will attend more 式 than you expect, and being able to read the程 of one — who speaks, when to clap, that the 乾杯 unfreezes the room — is worth more than any single grammar point in it.
exp.watch: April carries the year's thresholds: the school year and the corporate year both begin then, which is why 入学式 and 入社式 photographs both happen under cherry blossoms. That timing is institutional, not symbolic — the fiscal year drives it.

ex: 入社式にあたって、社長が挨拶をした。
At the entrance ceremony, the president gave an address.

exp.what: Write the first three lines of a ceremony speech: the occasion (にあたって／に際して), one ever-since line (て以来), and a thank-you.
exp.build: Shape to steal: 本日、〜にあたって、一言ご挨拶申し上げます。〜て以来、〜。皆様、ありがとうございます。
exp.when: The opener transfers to every formal setting — a toast, a first day, a farewell.
exp.watch: The occasion grammar carries the formality; the rest of the lines should stay plain or the speech turns to syrup.

ex: 本日、開店にあたって、一言ご挨拶申し上げます。
On the occasion of our opening today, allow me a brief word of greeting.

new_steps.note: Step 37 taught audience and coverage one noun at a time. This step is the wide-angle set: patterns that claim a whole range — regardless of, not only, spanning, throughout — the grammar of job postings, surveys and announcements.

exp.what: The recruiting-poster pattern: 年齢を問わず, regardless of age — the named category is declared irrelevant. 問わず is 問う (to ask) in the old negative you met in sb-zaru: 'without asking.'
exp.build: Noun + を問わず: 経験を問わず, 昼夜を問わず. The noun is usually a category with obvious alternatives — age, sex, experience, weather, day or night.
exp.when: Job ads, event announcements, product claims. 国籍を問わず on a hiring page is the sentence this step's vocabulary was chosen for.
exp.watch: The noun must be a dimension, not an individual: 田中さんを問わず fails because 田中さん isn't a category. And it lives in writing — spoken Japanese says に関係なく instead.

ex: 年齢や経験を問わず、どなたでも応募できます。
Anyone may apply, regardless of age or experience.
この店は昼夜を問わず、営業している。
This shop is open day and night.

exp.what: だけでなく climbed into formal dress. のみならず is 'not only X but also Y' for documents and news copy, and it expects the second half to widen the claim — smaller thing first, bigger thing after.
exp.build: Noun／plain clause + のみならず … も／まで: 学生のみならず教師も. のみ is the written だけ; ならず is the old negative again.
exp.when: Reports and articles. In speech it sounds recited — だけでなく still does the daily work.
exp.watch: Order matters: the のみならず half is the lesser, expected part; the も half is the surprise. Reversing them reads as bathos — 全国のみならず町内も deflates.

ex: この問題は日本のみならず、世界中で起きている。
This problem is happening not only in Japan but worldwide.
彼は英語のみならず、中国語も話せる。
He speaks not only English but Chinese too.

exp.what: A cousin of のみならず with a different center of gravity: X はもとより treats X as so obvious it barely needs saying, then adds Y on top. 平日はもとより週末も — weekdays go without saying; weekends too.
exp.build: Noun + はもとより … も: 味はもとより見た目も美しい. もとより means 'from the origin' — X was included from the start.
exp.when: Praising and describing scope: menus, reviews, introductions. Warmer and slightly less stiff than のみならず.
exp.watch: X must actually be obvious to the listener. Opening with a surprise (東京はもとより火星も) burns the pattern's whole premise — save the news for the も half.

ex: この旅館は料理はもとより、温泉も素晴らしい。
This inn — the food goes without saying, and the baths are superb too.
彼は国内はもとより、海外でも有名だ。
He is famous at home, naturally, and abroad as well.

exp.what: A range claimed edge to edge: 三日間にわたって, spanning three full days; 全国にわたって, across the whole country. The verb 渡る — to cross — is underneath: the event crosses the entire named span.
exp.build: Noun of span + にわたって（は rarely）, or にわたる before a noun: 十年にわたる研究. The noun must have extent — time, area, range, fields.
exp.when: News and reports, where scale is the story: works spanning decades, storms spanning regions, an interview series spanning five sessions.
exp.watch: It emphasises the WHOLE span, so small stretches ring false — 五分にわたって会議した is mock-epic. で and の間 handle ordinary durations without fanfare.

ex: 工事は三か月にわたって行われた。
The construction was carried out over a span of three months.
彼の研究は幅広い分野にわたっている。
His research spans a broad range of fields.

exp.what: Two jobs, one shape. Channel: 友人を通じて知り合った — we met through a friend. Duration: 一年を通じて暖かい — warm throughout the year. Both readings pass something through a medium: an introduction through a person, a climate through a calendar.
exp.build: Noun + を通じて or を通して — interchangeable in most uses; を通して leans slightly toward deliberate channels, を通じて toward coverage. Both prefer writing to chat.
exp.when: Explaining how you know someone, how information travelled, or that something held all year/period long — the two commonest N2 essay needs in one pattern.
exp.watch: For the duration sense the period must be complete: 一年を通じて claims all twelve months. If it only held in summer, the pattern has overclaimed and 夏の間 was the honest phrase.

ex: 仕事を通じて、多くの人と知り合った。
Through work, I've come to know many people.
この地方は一年を通して雨が少ない。
This region has little rain throughout the year.

exp.what: The scope-widener: 学生に限らず、誰でも参加できる — not limited to students; anyone can join. It takes a category the listener assumed was the boundary and erases the boundary.
exp.build: Noun + に限らず: 平日に限らず, 日本に限らず. Built on 限る, to limit — the same verb Step 47's sb will meet pointing the OTHER way.
exp.when: Announcements and corrections of assumption: the sale isn't just weekends, the rule isn't just beginners. Spoken and written both — this one, unlike を問わず, survives conversation.
exp.watch: It presupposes the listener expected the limit. Using it where no one assumed one (犬に限らず動物が好き, said apropos of nothing) sounds like answering a question nobody asked.

ex: この問題は若者に限らず、誰にでも関係がある。
This issue concerns everyone, not just the young.
週末に限らず、平日も混んでいる。
It's crowded on weekdays too, not just weekends.

points.jp: 限る一族 — に限って・に限り・に限らず

exp.what: One verb, three particles, three unrelated-looking meanings. に限らず widens (not limited to). に限り narrows officially (本日に限り, today only — coupon language). に限って does two strange things: picks the one exception (うちの子に限って, MY child would never) and marks cursed timing (急いでいる時に限って電車が遅れる — always exactly when I'm rushing).
exp.build: All three are Noun + the fixed form. Only に限らず takes the widening; only に限り belongs on posters; に限って carries the emotional readings.
exp.when: Reading them correctly matters more than producing: a coupon's に限り and a parent's に限って cannot be swapped, and the timing-lament に限って is one of the most Japanese sentences there is.
exp.watch: The two narrow forms split by register: に限り is official and cold; に限って is personal and hot. Mixing them — 本日に限って50%引き — turns a sale into a complaint about fate.

ex: 急いでいる日に限って、バスが来ない。
It's always the days I'm in a hurry that the bus doesn't come.
本日に限り、送料無料です。
Today only: free shipping.

exp.what: Write a four-line notice for an event or job: who may apply (を問わず／に限らず), the span (にわたって／を通じて), what's included (のみならず・はもとより), and the deadline.
exp.build: Shape to steal: 経験を問わず、どなたでも歓迎します。活動は一年を通じて行います。〆切は〜です。
exp.when: The notice register is half of written N2 — this is a rehearsal for reading a hundred of them.
exp.watch: Notices state scope, never enthusiasm. If your draft contains 楽しい, the register has slipped.

ex: 年齢・国籍を問わず、参加者を募集しています。
We are recruiting participants regardless of age or nationality.
